overview: These three atlas labels cover the same part of Lower Myanmar in 800 to 1000 and again in 1100 to 1279. Their outline includes Thaton, Winka, Kyaikkatha, Bago and Pathein, but excludes Pagan, central Thai Dvaravati and even some places in today’s Mon State. They are best read here as a regional Mon-history umbrella, not proof of one kingdom with unchanged borders. Early local polities, Mon-speaking communities under Pagan, and the later Hanthawaddy kingdom must remain distinct. The gap between the imported records does not mean that people vanished. Archaeological finds establish busy settlements more securely than they establish the language or ruler of every household.

periods.title: Early regional settlements
periods.summary: The first two imported records cover 800 to 1000. Thaton’s Buddhist tablets offer material evidence within a broader eighth-to-eleventh-century stylistic range, without proving a single state across the polygon.

periods.title: A gap in these map records
periods.summary: No member of this three-record group covers 1000 to 1100. The gap is an atlas feature, not an interruption of settlement or Mon-language history.

periods.title: A later regional label
periods.summary: The later record repeats the Lower Myanmar outline through 1279. Its label cannot establish independence from Pagan, and its cutoff is not a dated extinction of Mon communities.

items.text: The account of Anawrahta carrying Buddhist scriptures and captives from Thaton in 1057 comes from much later records, and its details are debated. Evidence includes Kyanzittha’s Mon inscriptions at Thaton and Winka, one dated 1098, recording religious repairs. These connect the region with Pagan’s kings rather than proving an independent Mon kingdom throughout the later map interval.

Excavations at Winka in the 1970s uncovered brick monastic residences and an octagonal stupa base faced with laterite. These remains place communal religious life in a built landscape. Monks needed living space as well as monuments; the surviving foundations reveal more than a royal name would.

Research at Catubhummika monastery in Thaton identified 1,350 well-preserved terracotta votive tablets alongside many fragments. Their Buddha images and architectural details suggest dates between roughly the eighth or ninth and eleventh centuries. Such small devotional objects can preserve a much larger history of religious activity beneath a site still used by a monastery.

Those tablets show individual Buddhas, groups of sacred figures and episodes from the Buddha’s life. The researcher compared their thrones, parasols and stupas with examples in India, Thailand, Java and other parts of Myanmar. Shared artistic ideas traveled far; resemblance alone cannot tell us whether a particular artist, pilgrim or merchant made the journey.

Kyaikkatha became visible to modern researchers through aerial photographs before ground investigation. Its ancient bricks bear straight, curved and sometimes wavy finger marks. Making and handling such heavy building material required practiced local work. The marks are intriguing traces of production, but similar bricks occur too widely to identify a maker’s ethnicity.

Pottery studies document red bowls at Winka, ochre-washed vessels at nearby Zothoke, and gritty, unglazed bowls and body fragments at Thaton. Paddle or mould impressions preserve clues to shaping clay. These everyday containers bring preparation, serving and storage into the story, although the finds do not by themselves reveal an exact menu or family size.

Researchers also examine ceramic chemistry to test connections between Myanmar and India. Similar mineral and elemental patterns can support hypotheses about transported pots or shared manufacturing practices. The study combines laboratory work with archaeological context, across a much longer period than this map. A broken bowl can be a useful clue, even when it has lost its matching dinner set.

At Kyaikkatha, seasonal ponds and channels lay within the settlement’s walls. A partly artificial lake and a chain of smaller reservoirs helped organize water in a landscape shaped by rain and changing levels. The surviving system includes a canal about one kilometer long. Its role suggests an early connection with settlement, but the researchers explicitly report that the canal lacks excavation and absolute dating.

Thaton’s old enclosure had two walls and a moat faced with laterite, a locally available building stone. Investigators also found finger-marked bricks near its southeastern wall and in surrounding villages. These remains show investment in constructing a town’s edges. A moat, however, is not evidence that every home had drains or toilets; household sanitation remains outside what these finds establish.

Several reservoirs near Kyaikkatha have recorded names meaning Elder Sister Lake, Younger Sister Lake and Mother Lake. The names make the landscape sound like a family gathering. They belong to the place-names documented by modern researchers; we do not know that residents used those same names during the medieval map period.

A Thaton stone tells the Mahajanaka story with the prince appearing twice: in a stormy sea and clinging to a broken mast. Its approximately eleventh-century carving turns one surface into successive scenes. Recognizing such stories offered a way to learn Buddhist narratives through pictures.

A Winka tablet preserves Mon words transcribed as “ḅār” and “kyāk,” translated “two” and “holy object” by linguist Mathias Jenny. These are surviving words, not a reconstructed sentence. The proposed sixth-century dating is disputed. This Roman transcription therefore illustrates an early inscription with uncertain chronology, not a securely dated sample from 800.

Later Mon royal authority appears clearly in a different setting. At Kyaikmaraw, southeast of Mawlamyine and outside this outline, an inscription records Queen Shin Sawbu of Pegu giving land to a shrine in 1455. This belongs to the later Hanthawaddy world. A woman could rule and direct substantial religious patronage, but her reign must not be moved backward into the earlier Thaton records.

Much later Mon medical manuscripts survive at Wat Cet Riw in Thailand’s Samut Sakhon province. The British Library describes accordion-fold paper books combining illness, the body and astrology, in Mon with Pali and other languages. Different handwriting, blank pages and doodles show books being added to over time. These nineteenth- and early twentieth-century materials illuminate later healing traditions, not medieval treatments in Thaton.

The same Thai-Mon community remembered branching from another nearby settlement and, earlier, from a village in Burma. A box holding manuscripts carried a donor list dated 1918, although the listed texts no longer survived there. Family and community memory, temple donations and copying kept cultural connections alive across borders; the box’s date does not date every book inside it.

ending.text: The atlas cutoffs of 900, 1000 and 1279 are not three documented falls of a single Mon kingdom. The later Pegu court’s Mon inscription of 1455 and the Thai-Mon manuscript communities illustrate different forms of continuity after the mapped periods. Governments and centers of power changed; Mon people and cultural life did not end with these outlines.
